description: Pause on approvals for data centers, battery energy storage systems, and similar utility-intensive industrial/technology uses while the city studies zoning and development standards. description: Regional energy grid infrastructure, high-voltage utility demand, and public safety concerns common to both data centers and battery energy storage systems; staff reported needing the full extended year to finish the data center ordinance after spending the prior year on the energy-storage-system framework. Active (extended) as of 2026-09-23. The County Board voted unanimously on August 18, 2026 to extend the moratorium on data centers (originally adopted August 2025) for a second consecutive year, through August 19, 2027, finding that allowing it to lapse would threaten public safety and orderly development because current regulations are inadequate. Planning and Zoning Administrator Trevor Bordelon said his office would need the full additional year to develop the data-center ordinance, having spent the prior year on a parallel energy-storage-system framework intended to serve as a foundation for high-load utility planning generally. Legal basis: Temporary interim zoning ordinance on data centers, adopted by the Freeborn County Board of Commissioners in August 2025 (alongside a parallel moratorium on energy storage systems, due to overlapping grid-infrastructure concerns); extended for a second year (through Aug. 19, 2027) by unanimous County Board resolution on August 18, 2026, under Minnesota Statutes Chapter 394.

description: Commissioners cited possible effects on water, power, noise, drainage, and public health from large new solar, wind, battery-storage, and data-center developments outside city limits, describing the pause as 'due diligence'; no specific project was pending at the time of adoption. Active as of 2026-09-23; set to expire 2027-09-08 absent a single permitted extension of up to six additional months. Residents and at least one local business owner (who called the measure 'backdoor zoning') have publicly questioned whether the county had legal authority to adopt it without voter-approved planning and zoning; commissioners have declined to comment publicly and the county's own attorney has not returned press inquiries. Legal basis: Cedar County ordinance imposing a 12-month moratorium, adopted by commissioners 2026-09-08, citing (among other authority) RSMo §49.650 and county public-health authority; legal commentators note §49.650 by its terms applies to first-, second-, and fourth-class noncharter counties while Cedar County is third class, raising an open legal question about the ordinance's validity.

description: Pause on accepting, processing, or issuing permits, licenses, and applications for new data centers and battery energy storage systems while the city develops zoning and regulatory standards. Active as of 2026-09-23 (the 180-day moratorium is set to run through 2027-01-02 absent extension). Permanent data-center/BESS zoning rules remain in process: the City Council discussed proposed new standards but pushed its final vote back at least a month after confusion among residents and councilmembers, with City Manager Troy Anderson confirming the moratorium itself is unaffected by that separate vote; Mayor Kevin King said he would look into organizing a public hearing before the council revisits the permanent rules in October 2026. Similar temporary pauses remain in effect in unincorporated Jackson County and neighboring Leavenworth County, Kansas. Legal basis: Resolution No. 7238 (City Council agenda item 26-741), 'A resolution declaring a 180-day moratorium on the processing of applications related to and issuance of city permits or licenses related to the installation or use of data processing and hosting facilities located in the City of Independence, Missouri, for projects or applications not already submitted to, authorized, or approved by the City,' sponsored by Councilmember Stewart and passed 7-0 on 2026-07-06. A companion Resolution No. 7239 (agenda item 26-742) imposed a parallel 180-day moratorium on battery energy storage system (BESS) facilities, also passed 7-0 the same night.

description: Rapid emergence of data center and battery energy storage system applications; perceived gaps in the Jackson County Unified Development Code; infrastructure, environmental, public safety, and public notice concerns. Adopted by the County Legislature (8 in favor, 1 excused) on 2026-06-22 as a 180-day moratorium on data-center and BESS land-use applications, for the purpose of developing long-term policy, County Code provisions, and enhanced public-notice requirements. Whether the measure was signed by County Executive Phil LeVota, became law without signature, or was vetoed was not independently confirmed in this pass; no veto was reported in any subsequent coverage found. Legal basis: Ordinance 6074, introduced 2026-04-06 by Legislator Sean E. Smith (120-day version); a competing 365-day version (Ordinance 6087, sponsored by Legislative Chair Manny Abarca) was also considered in committee as of 2026-06-01. The full County Legislature passed a 180-day moratorium on data-center and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) land-use applications by an 8-1 vote (one member excused) on 2026-06-22. Per KCTV5, the ordinance then went to County Executive Phil LeVota, who had 10 days to sign or veto; no veto was reported in subsequent coverage found in this pass, but the Executive's signature was not independently confirmed, and the exact ordinance/file number of the version that received final passage (whether an amended Ordinance 6074 or a substitute) was not confirmed from a primary Legistar record, which returned an access error to automated fetch.

description: Butler County has no zoning; a countywide survey (~800 responses) found roughly 90% support for a moratorium on the top land uses of concern (wind, solar, data centers, battery storage, landfill), following years of unregulated development including the in-progress Sandhills Energy solar project. Active as of 2026-09-23, though modified: adopted 2026-03-16 as a 9-month moratorium (through approximately 2026-12-15) on wind, solar, data center, battery storage, and landfill land uses while the county completes a comprehensive plan and zoning regulations (targeted for completion around September 2026). Per Flatwater Free Press, after the threat of a lawsuit the county later exempted the ongoing Sandhills Energy solar project (which had been under development since 2019) from the moratorium. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-07 (Butler County Board of Supervisors), mirroring the Planning Commission's Resolution 2026-04 but striking language that would have excluded projects already under construction.

description: Comprehensive health and safety review of AI data centers and battery energy storage systems. Active as of 2026-09-23. description: County currently lacks local zoning regulations for data centers, battery energy storage systems, or large-scale solar; officials cite fire hazards (BESS), noise/vibration from cooling units, light pollution, water/air quality, stormwater runoff, and traffic impacts. As of October 2022, the township’s zoning ordinance requires that wind turbines be set back at least 1,760 feet from property lines or 4 times tower height, whichever is greater, and limits shadow flicker to zero; it also limits the height of commercial solar energy systems to 12 feet and requires that they be set back 500 feet from property lines.

description: Amendments regulate utility-scale solar and wind projects with a cap of 500 acres and specific setbacks.
long_description: In June 2024 the Board of Supervisors voted unanimously in favor of amendments to the county’s Comprehensive Plan and Zoning Ordinance to regulate renewable energy facilities. The amendments define utility-scale solar projects as those with a capacity of 1 MW or greater and limit the total size of any such projects to 500 acres. The amendments further require that such projects be set back at least 1 mile from any town or city boundary and at least 2 miles from any existing solar project. Further, any solar projects interconnecting to the grid must be located within 2 miles of transmission line corridors.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (June 2025 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records.csv

description: Northeast Vermont Development Association unanimously approved a resolution against industrial-scale wind energy development.
long_description: In January 2015, the Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA) — one of eleven Vermont regional planning commissions — unanimously approved a resolution against the development of all industrial wind energy systems. description: Kittitas County Commissioners established a temporary moratorium on major solar energy projects.
long_description: In early 2017, the Kittitas County Commissioners established a temporary moratorium on applications for major solar energy projects. The moratorium was rescinded in October 2018 with the adoption of a new ordinance.

long_description: An ordinance adopted in April 2021 by the Town of Springfield sets out policies that discourage siting utility-scale solar farms on agricultural land. The restrictions are nonbinding.
